name: Passage de la Trinite
short_description: Site of the medieval Hôpital de la Trinité on rue Saint-Denis, birthplace of Parisian theatre where the first religious mysteries were staged in 1402

name: Tour Jean sans Peur
short_description: Paris's only surviving medieval military tower, built 1409-1411 by the Duc de Bourgogne as a defence against his enemies

name: Place du Caire
short_description: Small square with Egyptian-themed facade commemorating Napoleon's campaigns, site of the notorious medieval Cour des Miracles

name: Rue de Clery
short_description: Historic street in the Sentier district where Madame de Pompadour was born and Corneille spent his final years

name: Place de Louvois
short_description: Small square opposite the Bibliothèque Nationale, site of the Opera House where the Duc de Berry was assassinated in 1820

name: Synagogue Notre-Dame-de-Nazareth
short_description: The oldest of the 'great' synagogues of Paris, built in 1822 for the Ashkenazi community, rebuilt in 1852 with Rothschild funding.

name: 3 Rue Volta
short_description: A half-timbered house long claimed to be the oldest house in Paris, later dated to 1644.

name: Convent of the Madelonnettes
short_description: Former 1618 convent for 'fallen women' where Ninon de Lenclos was imprisoned; demolished 1865-66.

name: Wallace Fountain (Passage du Pont-aux-Biches)
short_description: One of Paris's iconic green drinking fountains donated by Sir Richard Wallace in the 1870s.

name: La Force Prison Site
short_description: Former prison where the Princesse de Lamballe was murdered during the September Massacres of 1792.

name: Rue de la Verrerie
short_description: Medieval street where playing cards were first painted for the mad King Charles VI.

name: Hotel Chalons de Luxembourg
short_description: 17th-century Marais mansion with a lion's head portal, where d'Annunzio once lived.

name: Verlaine's Garret
short_description: The miserable room at 39 rue Descartes where poet Paul Verlaine died on 8 January 1896.

name: Rue de l'Hirondelle
short_description: Medieval alley with a salamander-carved facade marking the love-nest of Francois I and Anne de Pisseleu.

name: Caveau de la Bolee
short_description: 13th-century cellar cabaret on rue de l'Hirondelle frequented by Baudelaire, Verlaine and Oscar Wilde.

name: Marché Saint-Germain
short_description: Covered market built on the site of the legendary medieval Foire Saint-Germain, destroyed by fire in 1762.

name: Café de la Mairie
short_description: Unassuming café on Place Saint-Sulpice frequented by Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Beckett; site of the last Sartre-Camus meeting in 1951.

name: Palais du Luxembourg
short_description: 17th-century palace built for Marie de Medici, now seat of the French Senate, housing Delacroix paintings in its library.

name: Musée du Luxembourg
short_description: Paris's first public museum, opened 1750 in the Luxembourg Palace's east wing, now an exhibition space in the orangery.

name: 27 Rue de Fleurus
short_description: Home of Gertrude Stein and Alice B. Toklas 1903–1938; legendary literary salon for American expatriates.

name: Rue Férou
short_description: Quiet street behind Saint-Sulpice where Hemingway lived 1926–1928 and Man Ray settled after 1951.

name: Fontaine Médicis
short_description: Romantic grotto fountain in the Luxembourg Gardens, built c. 1630, rebuilt 1864–1866; features Leda and the swan by Auguste Ottin.

name: Statue of Marshal Ney
short_description: Bronze statue by François Rude of Marshal Michel Ney, inaugurated 7 December 1853 near the corner of Avenue de l'Observatoire and Boulevard du Montparnasse.

name: Fontaine des Quatre-Parties-du-Monde
short_description: Monumental 1874 fountain by Jean-Baptiste Carpeaux in the Jardin Marco Polo on Avenue de l'Observatoire.

name: Rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs
short_description: Historic Left Bank street associated with Hemingway's sawmill apartment and a medieval quarry route under Catherine de Medici.

name: Ecole Alsacienne
short_description: Prestigious Parisian school founded 1874 by Alsatian Protestant academics at 109 rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs; André Gide was an early pupil.

name: College Stanislas
short_description: Traditional Catholic school in the 6th arr; notable alumni include a young Charles de Gaulle.

name: 3 Rue Joseph-Bara
short_description: Artists' studios at 3 rue Joseph-Bara, social hub of the Ecole de Paris in the 1920s; home to Kisling, Modigliani, Pascin.

name: Musee Zadkine
short_description: Studio-museum at 100 bis rue d'Assas dedicated to sculptor Ossip Zadkine (lived 1928–1967); free city museum.

name: Reid Hall
short_description: Historic American academic residence at 6 rue de Chevreuse; now a Columbia University global centre.

name: Academie de la Grande-Chaumiere
short_description: Celebrated independent art academy at 14 rue de la Grande-Chaumière, founded 1902; teachers included Bourdelle, later Giacometti and Léger.

name: 26 Rue Vavin (Sauvage Building)
short_description: Stepped-terrace apartment building at 26 rue Vavin designed by Henri Sauvage (1912–14), clad in white and blue ceramic tiles.

name: La Rotonde
short_description: Legendary Montparnasse café opened 1911 by Victor Libion; refuge for Modigliani, Lenin, Trotsky and the Ecole de Paris.

name: Quai Voltaire
short_description: Historic Left Bank embankment; Voltaire died at no. 27; Baudelaire, Wagner, Delacroix and Ingres all lived or worked here.

name: Fontaine des Quatre Saisons
short_description: Monumental 18th-century wall fountain at 57–59 rue de Grenelle, sculpted by Edme Bouchardon (1739–1745).

name: Saint-Thomas-d'Aquin
short_description: 17th-century Dominican church on Place Saint-Thomas-d'Aquin, parish church of returning aristocratic émigrés after the Revolution.

name: Le Bon Marché
short_description: The world's first modern department store, founded 1838 at 24 rue de Sèvres; inspiration for Zola's Au Bonheur des Dames.

name: La Pagode
short_description: Japanese-style pagoda cinema at 57 bis rue de Babylone, built 1895–96 by Alexandre Marcel; converted to cinema 1931.

name: Hotel Matignon
short_description: Official residence of the French Prime Minister since 1935; one of the grandest 18th-century mansions in the Faubourg Saint-Germain, with an immense private garden.

name: Musee de la Legion d'Honneur
short_description: Museum of medals, orders, and historical paraphernalia housed in the Hôtel de Salm, a neoclassical mansion set on fire during the Commune and beautifully restored.

name: Eglise Sainte-Clotilde
short_description: 19th-century neo-Gothic church in the 7th arrondissement, built by architects Gau and Ballu; famous as the church where César Franck served as organist for over 30 years.

name: Hotel de Gallifet
short_description: 18th-century mansion on rue de Grenelle once home to Talleyrand across four different regimes; now the Italian Cultural Institute and Italian Embassy since 1909.

name: Fontaine de Mars
short_description: Napoleonic-era neoclassical fountain at 129 rue Saint-Dominique depicting Mars and Hygeia, built 1806-1809.

name: Église Saint-Pierre du Gros Caillou
name_variations: Church of Saint-Pierre du Gros Caillou
short_description: Parish church at 92 rue Saint-Dominique, the 1822 successor to the original village church of the Gros Caillou neighbourhood.

name: Rue Cler
short_description: Pedestrianised market street in the 7th arrondissement, celebrated for its village atmosphere and daily produce market.

name: Ecole Militaire
short_description: 18th-century military academy on Avenue de la Motte-Picquet, commissioned by Louis XV with Madame de Pompadour's backing and designed by Gabriel.

name: UNESCO Headquarters Paris
short_description: UNESCO's Paris headquarters at Place de Fontenoy, a Y-shaped Modernist building (1958) by Breuer, Nervi, and Zehrfuss, with a Japanese garden by Isamu Noguchi.

name: Champ de Mars
short_description: Large public greenspace flanking the Eiffel Tower, formerly the parade ground of the Ecole Militaire and site of successive Expositions Universelles.

name: Square Jean XXIII
short_description: Cathedral garden on the south side of Notre-Dame, dedicated to the memory of Pope John XXIII (Angelo Roncalli), on the site of the former archbishop's palace destroyed in 1831.

name: Square Rene Viviani
short_description: Small Left Bank square adjacent to Saint-Julien-le-Pauvre, home to the oldest tree in Paris (a Robinia planted in 1601), with a bronze fountain depicting the legend of Saint-Julien.

name: Square Paul-Painleve
short_description: Small square on the south side of rue des Ecoles adjacent to the Musée de Cluny, featuring a bronze statue of Michel de Montaigne and flanked by Librairie Compagnie and Brasserie Balzar.

name: Square Paul-Langevin
short_description: Flower-bordered square beneath la Montagne Sainte-Geneviève named for physicist Paul Langevin, featuring a statue of François Villon and the ivy-covered rear wall of the former Ecole Polytechnique.

name: Jardin Carre
short_description: Serene topiary garden with a square pool at 11 rue Descartes, created in the courtyard of the original Ecole Polytechnique (1794), a public hideaway for Sorbonne academic families.

name: Jardin Alpin
short_description: Alpine Garden inside the Jardin des Plantes, accessed through a tunnel, with over 2,000 alpine plant species from across the world

name: Jardin Tino Rossi
short_description: Peaceful garden on Quai Saint-Bernard with summer evening dancing, adjacent to the open-air sculpture museum

name: Institut Catholique
short_description: Catholic university at 21, rue d'Assas; Flemish Gothic courtyard; 120 priests massacred 1792; Beauvoir and Maritain studied/taught here

name: 9 Quai Malaquais (George Sand)
short_description: George Sand's address 1832–1836; wrote Lélia here; began dressing in men's clothing to attend the opera

name: Cemetery of Eglise Saint-Germain de Charonne
Jardin Catherine-Laboure
short_description: Vegetable and flower garden on the grounds of the Sisters of Charity convent at 33 rue de Babylone, with an arbor; a haven for Parisians at lunchtime.

name: Hotel Lutetia
short_description: Historic Left Bank luxury hotel at 45 boulevard Raspail, requisitioned by German forces during the Occupation and used as a repatriation centre for POWs and concentration camp survivors after the Liberation.

name: Musée Eugène Delacroix
short_description: Apartment and studio-museum of Eugène Delacroix at 6, place de Furstemberg

name: Jardin de la Clinique Saint-Jean de Dieu
short_description: Hidden rose garden behind the Clinique Saint-Jean de Dieu hospital at 19 rue Oudinot, accessible during visiting hours; one of the finest rose gardens in Paris.

name: Square Boucicaut
short_description: Public square in the 7th arrondissement commemorating Aristide and Marguerite Boucicaut, founders of Le Bon Marché, with a sculpture of Madame Boucicaut at its entrance.

name: Jardins du Musee de Cluny
name_variations: Gardens of the Musée de Cluny
short_description: Medieval-themed enclosed gardens at the Musée de Cluny, arranged thematically around love, nature, and the soul, inspired by medieval hortus conclusus tradition.
